why_use_this: This is the general-purpose numerical-methods toolbox most other packages in the vani-* math ecosystem either depend on or duplicate a piece of ([vani-algebra](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-algebra), [vani-interval](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-interval), [vani-vectorcalc](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-vectorcalc) all reuse or mirror functions from here). Reach for it whenever you need to integrate, differentiate, find a root, minimize a 1D function, solve an ODE, work with polynomials, or interpolate between sample points, and a compiler builtin (`sin`, `exp`, `f64_erf`, ...) doesn't already cover it directly. For ODEs specifically: use the explicit solvers (`euler_solve`, `rk4_solve`, `rk45_step`) for well-behaved ("non-stiff") systems, but switch to the implicit solvers (`backward_euler_solve`, `crank_nicolson_solve`, `bdf2_solve`) for STIFF systems -- ones where the explicit solvers diverge or need an impractically tiny step size to stay stable, since the implicit methods are unconditionally stable (A-stable) at the cost of solving a small nonlinear equation via Newton's method at every step.

integrate_trapz.intuition: Approximate the area under a curve by chopping it into vertical strips and treating the top of each strip as a straight line (a trapezoid) instead of the curve's true shape -- simple, but a straight line can't perfectly track a curving function.
integrate_trapz.example: Integrate \(f(x)=x^2\) from \(0\) to \(2\) using \(n=2\) subintervals (\(h=1\)): sample points \(x=0,1,2\) give \(y=0,1,4\). \(\int\approx\dfrac12(0+2\times1+4)=\dfrac12(6)=3\). The true value is \(\int_0^2x^2dx=\left[\tfrac{x^3}3\right]_0^2=\tfrac83\approx2.667\) -- the trapezoidal estimate (\(3\)) OVERESTIMATES, because straight lines connecting points on an upward-curving (convex) function always sit above the true curve.
integrate_trapz.why: Compare this directly with `integrate_simpson`'s example on the exact same integral -- Simpson's rule (fitting parabolas instead of straight lines) gets the EXACT answer \(8/3\) using the very same 3 sample points, a concrete demonstration of why Simpson's rule is generally preferred when it's applicable.

integrate_simpson.intuition: Instead of connecting sample points with straight lines, fit a PARABOLA through each group of 3 consecutive points -- a much better match for a smoothly curving function, and exact whenever the true function IS (at most) a cubic.
integrate_simpson.example: Same integral as `integrate_trapz`'s example, \(f(x)=x^2\) on \([0,2]\), \(n=2\) (\(h=1\)), same sample points \(y=0,1,4\): \(\int\approx\dfrac13(0+4\times1+4)=\dfrac13(8)=\dfrac83\approx2.667\) -- EXACTLY matching the true value \(8/3\), not just approximating it.
integrate_simpson.why: This exactness isn't a coincidence -- Simpson's rule is built to be exact for any polynomial of degree 3 or lower, and \(x^2\) certainly qualifies. Compare with `integrate_trapz`'s answer of \(3\) on the identical problem: same number of function evaluations, but Simpson's rule gets the EXACT answer while the trapezoidal rule is off by about 12%.

integrate_romberg.intuition: Run the trapezoidal rule at a couple of different step sizes, then use the PATTERN of how the estimate changes as the step size shrinks to extrapolate toward what the answer would be at an infinitely fine step size -- squeezing much higher accuracy out of the same cheap trapezoidal estimates.
integrate_romberg.formula: Build a triangular table of trapezoidal estimates at halved step sizes, then Richardson-extrapolate across the table.
integrate_romberg.example: For \(f(x)=x^2\) on \([0,2]\): the crudest trapezoidal estimate (\(n=1\), \(h=2\), just the two endpoints \(y=0,4\)) is \(\dfrac22(0+4)=4\). The finer one (\(n=2\), \(h=1\)) is \(3\) (from `integrate_trapz`'s example). Richardson extrapolation combines them: \(R = \dfrac{4T(n{=}2)-T(n{=}1)}{3} = \dfrac{4\times3-4}{3}=\dfrac{8}{3}\approx2.667\) -- the EXACT answer, extrapolated from two estimates that were each individually wrong (\(4\) and \(3\)).
integrate_romberg.why: This is the same "combine two lower-order estimates to cancel out the leading error term" idea `bdf2_step` uses for ODEs, applied here to integration instead -- neither individual trapezoidal estimate was exact, but the specific combination \((4T_2-T_1)/3\) exactly cancels the error term that trapezoidal integration is known to have, for this smooth-enough function.

integrate_gauss_legendre_5.intuition: Instead of using evenly-spaced sample points, place the 5 sample points at specific, carefully chosen (unevenly-spaced) locations, and weight each one's contribution unevenly too -- these particular "magic" locations and weights are mathematically derived to make the result exact for polynomials up to degree 9, far beyond what 5 evenly-spaced points could achieve.
integrate_gauss_legendre_5.formula: \[ \int_a^b f\,dx \approx \dfrac{b-a}2\sum_{i=1}^5w_if(x_i) \] using the fixed Gauss-Legendre nodes/weights on \([-1,1]\), mapped onto \([a,b]\).
integrate_gauss_legendre_5.example: For \(f(x)=x^2\) on \([0,2]\) (the same integral `integrate_trapz`/`integrate_simpson` used): since \(x^2\) is only degree 2, far below this method's exactness threshold of degree 9, `integrate_gauss_legendre_5` also returns the exact \(8/3\), just like `integrate_simpson` did -- the extra accuracy headroom isn't visible on such a simple test function.
integrate_gauss_legendre_5.why: The real advantage over Simpson's rule shows up on functions that AREN'T low-degree polynomials -- for a genuinely complicated smooth function, 5 well-placed Gauss-Legendre points can match or beat the accuracy of many more evenly-spaced Simpson points, since it's exact for a much higher-degree polynomial approximation of the true function.

integrate_adaptive_trapz.intuition: Rather than deciding on a uniform grid density in advance, this checks its own accuracy as it goes: if a whole interval's trapezoidal estimate roughly agrees with the sum of its two half-interval estimates, stop there; if they disagree noticeably, that's a sign the function is doing something interesting in that region, so recurse into both halves for a closer look.
integrate_adaptive_trapz.formula: Compare the whole-interval trapezoidal estimate against the sum of the two half-interval estimates; accept if they agree within `tol`, else recurse into both halves.
integrate_adaptive_trapz.example: For \(f(x)=x^2\) on \([0,2]\): the whole-interval estimate (\(n=1\)) is \(4\) (from `integrate_romberg`'s example). The two half-interval estimates: \([0,1]\) gives \(\dfrac12(f(0)+f(1))=\dfrac12(0+1)=0.5\); \([1,2]\) gives \(\dfrac12(f(1)+f(2))=\dfrac12(1+4)=2.5\); sum \(=0.5+2.5=3\). Compare \(4\) (whole) against \(3\) (halves): they differ by \(1\) -- if that's larger than the caller's tolerance, this function would recurse into \([0,1]\) and \([1,2]\) separately, refining further.
integrate_adaptive_trapz.why: This concentrates the EXTRA work (more, smaller subintervals) exactly where the function is curving the most (where the whole-vs-halves comparison disagrees most), rather than wasting effort adding more sample points to regions where the function is already nearly linear and a coarse estimate is already accurate enough.

diff_central.intuition: Look at the function's value a little bit BEFORE and a little bit AFTER the point of interest, and use the slope of the line connecting those two nearby points as an estimate of the true instantaneous slope AT the point -- looking both ways cancels out more of the approximation error than looking only one way.
diff_central.why: Compare with `diff_forward`'s example on the exact same function and point: forward difference gives \(12.61\), noticeably further from the true \(12\) than central difference's \(12.01\) -- for the same step size \(h\), central difference's error shrinks quadratically (\(O(h^2)\)) while forward difference's error only shrinks linearly (\(O(h)\)), which is exactly the gap visible in these two numbers.

diff_forward.intuition: Only look FORWARD from the point of interest -- necessary when you can't evaluate the function below \(x\) at all (e.g. right at the edge of the domain, where `diff_central` would need a point that doesn't exist).
diff_forward.example: For \(f(x)=x^3\) at \(x=2\) with \(h=0.1\): \(f(2.1)=9.261\), \(f(2)=8\). \(f'(2)\approx\dfrac{9.261-8}{0.1}=\dfrac{1.261}{0.1}=12.61\) -- noticeably further from the true \(12\) than `diff_central`'s \(12.01\) using the same \(h\).
diff_forward.why: This one-sided approach is strictly less accurate than looking both ways for the SAME step size -- only reach for it when you genuinely can't evaluate \(f\) on one side (a domain boundary), not as a default choice.

diff_second.intuition: The same central-differencing idea as `diff_central`, one derivative order up -- comparing a point to the AVERAGE of its two neighbors (rather than just the difference of the neighbors) captures curvature instead of slope.
diff_second.why: This particular stencil happens to be exact for any CUBIC function (like \(x^3\) here) -- its leading error term involves the function's 4th derivative, which is identically zero for a cubic. This same 3-point stencil is what [vani-vectorcalc](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-vectorcalc)'s `vc_laplacian_2d` and [vani-pde](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-pde)'s heat/Laplace solvers build their multi-dimensional versions on top of.

bisect.intuition: If a continuous function is negative at one point and positive at another, it MUST cross zero somewhere between them (you can't get from negative to positive without passing through zero) -- so repeatedly checking the midpoint and keeping whichever half still shows this sign change guarantees you're always closing in on a real root.
bisect.formula: Given \(f(a)\) and \(f(b)\) with opposite signs, repeatedly bisect and keep the half still bracketing a sign change.
bisect.example: Find \(\sqrt2\) as a root of \(f(x)=x^2-2\), starting bracket \([1,2]\): \(f(1)=-1\), \(f(2)=2\), opposite signs, valid bracket. Midpoint \(1.5\): \(f(1.5)=0.25\), positive -- so the root is in \([1,1.5]\) (keep the half where the sign still changes, from \(f(1)=-1\) to \(f(1.5)=0.25\)). Next midpoint \(1.25\): \(f(1.25)=-0.4375\), negative -- root is in \([1.25,1.5]\). The bracket has narrowed from width \(1\) to width \(0.25\) in just two steps, already closing in on the true \(\sqrt2\approx1.41421\).
bisect.why: Every single step is GUARANTEED to halve the bracket, no matter how badly-behaved \(f\) is elsewhere -- this reliability is bisection's whole appeal, at the cost of being the slowest of this package's root-finders (compare `newton`'s example below, which gets much closer to \(\sqrt2\) in a single step, but without bisection's ironclad guarantee).

secant.intuition: Newton's method needs an exact derivative; the secant method fakes one using the slope of the line through the two most RECENT points instead -- no calculus required, just the function's own values.
secant.example: Same problem, \(f(x)=x^2-2\), starting from \(x_0=1\), \(x_1=2\) (\(f(x_0)=-1\), \(f(x_1)=2\)): \(x_2 = 2 - 2\times\dfrac{2-1}{2-(-1)} = 2-2\times\dfrac13 = 2-0.667=1.333\). \(f(1.333)\approx1.777-2=-0.222\) -- already noticeably closer to the true root \(\sqrt2\approx1.41421\) than either starting point.
secant.why: Secant needs no derivative at all (useful when one isn't available or is expensive to compute), and converges FASTER than bisection in practice (superlinear, order \(\approx1.618\)) -- but unlike bisection, it has NO convergence guarantee; a poorly-chosen starting pair can cause it to diverge or behave erratically.

newton.intuition: Use the function's actual slope at the current guess to jump directly toward where that TANGENT LINE crosses zero -- if the function is well-approximated by its tangent line near the root (usually true once you're reasonably close), this converges dramatically faster than bisection or the secant method.
newton.example: Same problem, \(f(x)=x^2-2\), \(f'(x)=2x\), starting from \(x_0=1.5\): \(f(1.5)=0.25\), \(f'(1.5)=3\). \(x_1 = 1.5 - 0.25/3 = 1.5-0.0833=1.4167\) -- already within \(0.003\) of the true \(\sqrt2\approx1.41421\), after just ONE step, starting from a cruder guess than `secant`'s example used.
newton.why: This dramatic single-step improvement is quadratic convergence in action -- each additional Newton step roughly SQUARES the number of correct digits, once you're close enough to the root. The catch (unlike bisection) is that nothing guarantees this good behavior from an arbitrary starting point; a bad initial guess can cause Newton's method to diverge or cycle forever.

brent.intuition: Gets the best of both worlds: use the fast methods (secant, or inverse quadratic interpolation) when they're working well, but fall back to a guaranteed bisection step whenever the fast method's suggested next point would leave the known bracket or isn't converging fast enough -- so it's never slower than bisection, but often much faster.
brent.formula: Combines bisection's guaranteed convergence with secant/inverse-quadratic interpolation's speed, falling back to bisection when the faster step isn't trustworthy.
brent.example: On the same \(f(x)=x^2-2\) problem, Brent's method would behave like `secant`'s fast-converging example above whenever the secant step stays safely within the current bracket, but would fall back to `bisect`'s guaranteed-safe halving step (like the example above) if a secant step ever tried to jump outside the known \([1,2]\) bracket.
brent.why: This is the ONLY one of this package's root-finders with BOTH a convergence guarantee AND fast typical-case performance -- reach for it by default when you have a valid bracket and don't have a specific reason to prefer a simpler method.

golden_section.intuition: To narrow down a minimum's location without any derivative information, evaluate the function at two carefully-placed interior points; the specific placement (the golden ratio) is chosen so that after discarding the worse side, ONE of the two interior points can be reused directly in the next round -- saving a function evaluation every single iteration.
golden_section.formula: Place two interior points at the golden ratio \(\varphi=(\sqrt5-1)/2\approx0.618\) fraction of the bracket, discard the side that doesn't contain the minimum.
golden_section.example: For \(f(x)=(x-2)^2+1\) (minimum at \(x=2\)) on bracket \([0,5]\): the two golden-ratio interior points sit at roughly \(x\approx1.91\) and \(x\approx3.09\) (placed symmetrically using the \(0.618\) ratio). Since \(f\) is symmetric around \(x=2\) and both points are nearly equidistant from it, \(f(1.91)\) and \(f(3.09)\) come out nearly equal -- either could be discarded, narrowing the bracket while keeping the OTHER point for direct reuse next round.
golden_section.why: The specific golden-ratio placement is what guarantees the reusable-point property -- ANY other split fraction would require evaluating the function at TWO brand-new points every iteration instead of just one, roughly doubling the total number of function evaluations needed for the same precision.

brent_min.intuition: The minimization analog of `brent`'s root-finding combination: use fast parabolic interpolation (fit a parabola through 3 points and jump to ITS minimum) when it looks trustworthy, fall back to golden-section search's guaranteed bracket-narrowing otherwise.
brent_min.formula: Combines golden-section search's guarantee with parabolic interpolation's speed when the function looks locally quadratic.
brent_min.example: For \(f(x)=(x-2)^2+1\) -- a function that IS exactly a parabola everywhere -- parabolic interpolation through any 3 points would jump directly to the exact minimum \(x=2\) in a single step, no golden-section fallback ever needed; Brent's method would recognize this immediately and converge about as fast as `newton_min`'s one-step example below.
brent_min.why: Real-world objectives are rarely EXACTLY quadratic everywhere the way this simple test function is -- Brent's method's real value shows up on functions that are only APPROXIMATELY quadratic near their minimum, where parabolic interpolation helps a lot but can't be blindly trusted far from the minimum, which is exactly when the golden-section fallback kicks in.

newton_min.intuition: A minimum is exactly where the derivative is zero -- so apply Newton's ROOT-FINDING method to \(f'\) instead of \(f\) itself, using the second derivative (the derivative of \(f'\)) the same way plain Newton's method uses the first derivative.
newton_min.example: For \(f(x)=(x-2)^2+1\): \(f'(x)=2(x-2)\), \(f''(x)=2\) (constant). Starting from \(x_0=0\): \(f'(0)=2(0-2)=-4\). \(x_1 = 0 - (-4)/2 = 0+2=2\) -- the EXACT minimum, reached in a single step.
newton_min.why: This is exact in one step because \(f\) is PURELY quadratic here, the same reason [vani-optimize](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-optimize)'s `newton_nd` reaches its sphere-function test case's minimum in one step too -- for a genuinely non-quadratic function, this would still converge fast (quadratically) near the minimum, but wouldn't finish in a single step.

euler_solve.intuition: The simplest possible way to step an ODE forward: look at the current slope, and walk in a straight line along that slope for one step's worth of time -- cheap, but if the true solution curves noticeably within that one step, the straight-line approximation drifts away from the truth.
euler_solve.example: Solve \(y'=y\), \(y(0)=1\) (whose exact solution is \(y(t)=e^t\)) for one step with \(h=0.1\): \(y_1 = y_0+h\times f(0,y_0) = 1+0.1\times1=1.1\). The true value is \(y(0.1)=e^{0.1}\approx1.10517\) -- Euler's estimate (\(1.1\)) is close but noticeably UNDER the true value.
euler_solve.why: Compare directly with `rk4_solve`'s example on the identical problem: RK4 gets \(1.105171\), matching the true \(e^{0.1}\) to 6 decimal places using the SAME step size \(h=0.1\) -- a dramatic accuracy difference for the same step cost, which is exactly why RK4 is the more commonly reached-for general-purpose explicit solver.

rk4_solve.intuition: Instead of using just the slope at the START of the step (like Euler), sample the slope at several cleverly-chosen points ACROSS the step (start, two different estimates at the midpoint, and the end) and combine them in a weighted average -- capturing much more of how the solution actually curves within the step.
rk4_solve.why: Four function evaluations per step (versus Euler's one) buys FOURTH-order accuracy (error shrinks as \(h^4\)) instead of Euler's first-order accuracy (error shrinks only as \(h\)) -- for smooth, well-behaved problems, this trade is almost always worth it, which is why RK4 is the standard general-purpose explicit ODE solver.

rk45_step.intuition: Compute BOTH a 4th-order and a 5th-order estimate from one batch of function evaluations -- the two estimates should nearly agree if the current step size is small enough for the solution's local behavior, so their DIFFERENCE is a built-in, nearly-free measure of how trustworthy this step actually is.
rk45_step.formula: Two different-order weighted combinations of the same set of function evaluations; their difference estimates local error.
rk45_step.example: For the same \(y'=y\) problem, both the 4th- and 5th-order estimates at \(h=0.1\) would land extremely close to the true \(e^{0.1}\approx1.105171\) (since this problem is smooth and well-behaved at this step size) -- their difference would come out tiny, signaling that this step size is more than adequate for the desired accuracy.
rk45_step.why: A caller doing ADAPTIVE step-size control would shrink \(h\) if this difference came out too large (signaling the current step is too coarse to trust) and could grow \(h\) if the difference is far smaller than needed (signaling wasted effort at an unnecessarily fine step) -- this function itself just returns the step's value, leaving that adaptive-control decision to the caller.

adams_bashforth_2.intuition: RK4 evaluates the function fresh, several times, every single step -- wasteful if you already computed a perfectly good \(f\) value at the PREVIOUS step and it's still lying around. This method reuses that previous value instead of re-deriving fresh intermediate points, at the cost of needing an extra bootstrap step to get started (there's no "previous" value before the very first step).
adams_bashforth_2.example: Continuing the \(y'=y\) problem with \(h=0.1\): using \(f_{\text{prev}}=f(0,1)=1\) and \(f_{\text{curr}}=f(0.1,1.105171)=1.105171\) (from `rk4_solve`'s accurate result): \(y_2 = 1.105171+\dfrac{0.1}2(3\times1.105171-1) = 1.105171+0.05\times2.315513=1.105171+0.115776=1.220947\). True value \(y(0.2)=e^{0.2}\approx1.221403\) -- close, though not as tight a match as RK4 achieved, using only ONE fresh function evaluation this step instead of RK4's four.
adams_bashforth_2.why: This is the classic multistep-method tradeoff: cheaper per step (one evaluation instead of four) in exchange for somewhat lower accuracy at the same step size, AND the added bookkeeping requirement of needing a separate single-step method (like `euler_solve` or one RK4 step) to bootstrap the very first step, since there's no "previous" \(f\) value before it.

backward_euler_step.intuition: Forward Euler uses the slope at the START of the step; backward Euler instead uses the slope at the END of the step it's trying to compute -- which sounds circular (you need to know \(y_{n+1}\) to compute the slope AT \(y_{n+1}\)), and it is: this makes \(y_{n+1}\) the solution to a small equation that has to be solved (via Newton's method here), not just read off directly.
backward_euler_step.example: For \(y'=y\) (so \(f(t,y)=y\)), this becomes \(y_1=y_0+hy_1\), i.e. \(y_1(1-h)=y_0\), solvable directly here since \(f\) is linear: \(y_1=y_0/(1-h) = 1/(1-0.1)=1/0.9\approx1.1111\). Compare to the true \(e^{0.1}\approx1.10517\): backward Euler OVERshoots slightly, the opposite direction from forward Euler's UNDERshoot (\(1.1\), from `euler_solve`'s example) on the identical problem.
backward_euler_step.why: Forward Euler underestimating and backward Euler overestimating (for this particular growing-exponential problem) is a nice illustration of why `crank_nicolson_step` -- which AVERAGES the two endpoints' slopes -- tends to land between the two and closer to the truth: see its own worked example, which lands almost exactly on \(1.105171\).

crank_nicolson_step.intuition: Rather than using EITHER the start-of-step slope (forward Euler) or the end-of-step slope (backward Euler) alone, average the two -- since one tends to undershoot and the other tends to overshoot (as `euler_solve`'s and `backward_euler_step`'s examples show), averaging them often lands much closer to the truth.
crank_nicolson_step.example: For \(y'=y\): \(y_1=y_0+\tfrac{h}2(y_0+y_1) = 1+0.05(1+y_1)\). Solving: \(y_1-0.05y_1=1.05\Rightarrow0.95y_1=1.05\Rightarrow y_1\approx1.1053\) -- MUCH closer to the true \(e^{0.1}\approx1.105171\) than either forward Euler's \(1.1\) or backward Euler's \(1.1111\) alone.
crank_nicolson_step.why: This averaging is exactly what buys Crank-Nicolson its second-order accuracy (versus backward Euler's first order) while KEEPING backward Euler's unconditional stability -- the best of both worlds for a stiff problem, at roughly the same per-step cost (still one implicit Newton solve).

bdf2_step.intuition: Instead of averaging endpoint slopes (Crank-Nicolson's approach), fit a polynomial through the last few known points and use ITS derivative structure to predict the next one -- a different route to the same second-order-accurate, unconditionally-stable destination.
bdf2_step.example: Continuing \(y'=y\) with \(h=0.1\), using \(y_{\text{prev}}=y(0)=1\) and \(y_{\text{curr}}=1.1111\) (from `backward_euler_step`'s bootstrap): \(y_{\text{next}} = \tfrac43(1.1111)-\tfrac13(1)+\tfrac{0.2}3y_{\text{next}}\). Solving for \(y_{\text{next}}\): \(y_{\text{next}}(1-0.0667) = 1.4815-0.3333=1.1482\), so \(y_{\text{next}}\approx1.2302\). True value \(y(0.2)=e^{0.2}\approx1.2214\) -- reasonably close, in the same accuracy class as `crank_nicolson_step`'s result.
bdf2_step.why: Notice this needed TWO prior points (\(y_{\text{prev}}\) and \(y_{\text{curr}}\)) to take a single step -- which is exactly why `bdf2_solve` has to bootstrap its very first step using `backward_euler_step` (a method that only needs one prior point), the same two-prior-points requirement `adams_bashforth_2` has for a completely different (explicit, not implicit) reason.

poly_eval.intuition: Rather than computing each power \(x,x^2,x^3,\ldots\) separately (wasteful -- each one could reuse the previous), factor the polynomial into nested multiplications: \(c_0+c_1x+c_2x^2 = c_0+x(c_1+xc_2)\), evaluated from the inside out.
poly_eval.example: Evaluate \(p(x)=2x^2+3x+1\) at \(x=2\) via Horner's method: start with the leading coefficient \(2\); multiply by \(x\) and add the next coefficient: \(2\times2+3=7\); multiply by \(x\) again and add the last coefficient: \(7\times2+1=15\). Direct check: \(2(2)^2+3(2)+1=8+6+1=15\) -- matches.
poly_eval.why: This costs exactly \(n\) multiply-adds for a degree-\(n\) polynomial, versus a naive approach that computes each power \(x^i\) from scratch (\(O(n^2)\) total multiplications, or \(O(n\log n)\) with fast exponentiation per term) -- Horner's method is both simpler to implement AND asymptotically cheaper.

poly_deriv_coeffs.intuition: The power rule (\(d(x^i)/dx = ix^{i-1}\)) applied to each term of the polynomial independently, all at once -- no numeric evaluation needed, just a mechanical rewrite of the coefficient list.
poly_deriv_coeffs.example: For \(p(x)=1+3x+2x^2\) (coefficients \([1,3,2]\)): the derivative's coefficients are \(c'_0=1\times c_1=3\) and \(c'_1=2\times c_2=4\), giving \(p'(x)=3+4x\) (coefficients \([3,4]\)). Direct check via ordinary calculus: \(d(1+3x+2x^2)/dx = 3+4x\) -- matches.
poly_deriv_coeffs.why: The constant term \(c_0=1\) simply disappears (a constant's derivative is always 0) and every remaining term's exponent drops by one -- this returns the ENTIRE derivative polynomial's coefficients at once, unlike `diff_central`/`diff_forward`, which only estimate a derivative's NUMERIC VALUE at one specific point.

poly_mul.intuition: Multiplying two polynomials means every term of one multiplies every term of the other, and terms with the SAME resulting power get added together -- exactly the schoolbook "multiply everything out and collect like terms" process, done systematically.
poly_mul.why: This is the exact same convolution pattern [vani-bignum](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-bignum)'s `bn_mul` uses for big-integer multiplication -- a polynomial's coefficients and a big number's base-\(10^9\) limbs are both just "a sequence of digits/coefficients combined via convolution", the same underlying math applied to two different domains.

lagrange_interp.intuition: There's exactly ONE polynomial of the right degree that passes through a given set of points -- this formula builds it as a weighted sum, where each given \(y\)-value gets a specially-constructed weight function that equals \(1\) at its own point and \(0\) at every other given point.
lagrange_interp.why: Because a quadratic is uniquely determined by exactly 3 points, Lagrange interpolation recovers it EXACTLY here -- but with MANY points, Lagrange interpolation can oscillate wildly between the given points (Runge's phenomenon), which is exactly why `cubic_spline_natural`'s example below shows a genuinely different (and for many points, better-behaved) answer on a similar problem.

cubic_spline_natural.intuition: Instead of one single high-degree polynomial through every point (which can wiggle unpredictably between points, especially with many of them), fit a SEPARATE cubic curve between each consecutive pair of points, carefully matched up so the value, slope, AND curvature all agree exactly where neighboring pieces meet -- a smooth, well-behaved patchwork instead of one wild global curve.
cubic_spline_natural.formula: Solve a tridiagonal system for each knot's second derivative \(M_i\), with the "natural" boundary condition \(M_0=M_{n-1}=0\) (zero curvature at both ends).
cubic_spline_natural.example: Using the SAME 3 points as `lagrange_interp`'s example, \((0,1)\), \((1,2)\), \((2,5)\) (uniform spacing \(h=1\)): the natural boundary conditions fix \(M_0=M_2=0\). The one interior equation (for the middle knot) is \(2(h+h)M_1 = 6\left[\dfrac{y_2-y_1}{h}-\dfrac{y_1-y_0}{h}\right]\), i.e. \(4M_1 = 6[(5-2)-(2-1)]=6[3-1]=12\), giving \(M_1=3\).
cubic_spline_natural.why: Compare `cubic_spline_eval`'s worked example, which evaluates THIS spline at \(x=0.5\) and gets \(1.3125\) -- noticeably DIFFERENT from `lagrange_interp`'s exact match to the true quadratic (\(f(0.5)=1.25\)) at the corresponding point. The natural spline's zero-curvature boundary condition is an ASSUMPTION about the endpoints that doesn't match this particular true function's actual (nonzero, constant) curvature -- a real reminder that "natural" is a specific modeling choice, not automatically the most accurate one for every underlying function.

cubic_spline_eval.intuition: Once the spline's knot second-derivatives are known (`cubic_spline_natural`'s job), evaluating at a specific query point just means finding which piece it falls into, then plugging into that one piece's cubic formula using its two endpoint values and their second derivatives.
cubic_spline_eval.formula: Find the interval \([x_i,x_{i+1}]\) containing \(x\) (via binary search), then evaluate that interval's cubic piece using \(y_i,y_{i+1},M_i,M_{i+1}\).
cubic_spline_eval.example: Evaluate `cubic_spline_natural`'s spline (\(M_0=0,M_1=3\), from its own example) at \(x=0.5\), which falls in \([x_0,x_1]=[0,1]\): using the standard cubic-piece formula with \(h=1\), the result comes out to \(1.3125\).
cubic_spline_eval.why: See `cubic_spline_natural`'s own "why" note for what this \(1.3125\) reveals -- it's noticeably different from the true underlying quadratic's actual value \(1.25\) at this point, a concrete illustration that the natural spline's boundary assumption trades some accuracy for a specific kind of smoothness guarantee.

kahan_sum.intuition: When you add a tiny number to a very large one in ordinary floating-point arithmetic, the tiny number's contribution can be completely lost -- there simply aren't enough digits of precision to represent both the huge number's magnitude AND the tiny addition at the same time. Kahan summation keeps a separate "what got rounded away" tally and feeds it back in on later additions, recovering precision that a naive running sum would silently throw away.
kahan_sum.formula: Accumulate a running sum while separately tracking and re-injecting the rounding error lost at each addition step.
kahan_sum.example: The classic illustration: summing \(10^{20}+1-10^{20}\) left to right in ordinary double-precision arithmetic. \(10^{20}+1\) rounds right back down to exactly \(10^{20}\) (since \(1\) is far too small relative to \(10^{20}\) to affect double precision's roughly 15-17 significant digits) -- so a naive running sum computes \((10^{20}+1)-10^{20} = 10^{20}-10^{20}=0\), the WRONG answer (the true sum is \(1\)). Kahan summation's compensation term tracks that lost \(+1\) separately and correctly recovers it, giving the right answer, \(1\).
kahan_sum.why: This kind of precision loss is invisible until it silently corrupts a result -- Kahan summation costs a small constant amount of extra bookkeeping per addition, in exchange for dramatically more reliable results whenever you're summing many numbers of wildly different magnitudes, exactly the scenario this example is built around.

running_mean_update.intuition: You don't need to remember every previous sample to keep an accurate running average -- just nudge the current mean toward the new sample by an amount that shrinks as more samples accumulate (each new sample should matter less to the overall average the more samples you've already seen).
running_mean_update.example: Samples arrive one at a time: \(4\), then \(6\), then \(8\). After the first sample, mean is \(4\). After the second (\(n=2\), \(x=6\)): \(\bar x_2 = 4+\dfrac{6-4}{2}=4+1=5\) -- check directly: \((4+6)/2=5\), matches. After the third (\(n=3\), \(x=8\)): \(\bar x_3=5+\dfrac{8-5}{3}=5+1=6\) -- check: \((4+6+8)/3=18/3=6\), matches.
running_mean_update.why: This never needs to re-sum the whole history -- each update is \(O(1)\) regardless of how many samples came before, useful for streaming data where storing every past value would be impractical, the same streaming philosophy [vani-probability](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-probability)'s Welford variance-update functions apply to variance instead of just the mean.
